title: Alterations in the Immune‐Fibrotic Axis Are Spatially Localized in the Aging Heart

paragraphs.en: Aging poses one of the major risk factors for cardiovascular disease. In the mammalian heart, a persistent inflammatory state known as inflammaging is promoted by various repeated antigenic stimuli throughout life, driving the release of chronic low‐grade inflammatory signals (Ferrucci and Fabbri 2018). Cardiovascular inflammaging is associated with fibrosis, vascular dysfunction and impaired tissue homeostasis that together promote adverse cardiac remodeling, atherosclerosis, and heart failure (Chirinos et al. 2019; Liberale et al. 2025). Age‐related changes in cardiomyocyte function (Yucel et al. 2026) and the perivascular environment (Rodriguez Morales et al. 2025) include the accumulation of cells with senescence‐associated features defined by a set of hallmarks that includes cell‐cycle arrest (Abdellatif et al. 2023; Gorgoulis et al. 2019; SenNet Consortium 2022).

Cardiovascular inflammaging is driven primarily by a shift in immune and resident stromal cell interactions. In the adult heart, resident macrophages contribute to maintaining homeostasis by clearing pathogens and debris and influence fibrosis by interacting with other cells through antigen presentation, cytokine and chemokine signaling (Nicolas‐Avila et al. 2022). With advanced age, self‐sustaining protective resident macrophages are replaced by aggressive bone marrow‐derived macrophages that stoke chronic tissue inflammation. Adult cardiac fibroblasts retain an organ‐specific embryonic transcriptome (Forte et al. 2022; Furtado et al. 2016) and are normally responsible for routine extracellular matrix (ECM) maintenance by responding to biochemical and mechanical signals within the myocardium (Pesce et al. 2023; Tallquist and Molkentin 2017). In aged hearts, cardiac fibroblasts are induced by pro‐inflammatory macrophages to become chronically overactive, secreting cytokines and matrix‐remodeling proteins and driving localized fibrosis that recruits more immune cells, which accelerates tissue stiffening and functional decline (Frangogiannis 2019).

Collectively, inflammaging affects coordination among cardiac cell populations: activated macrophages contribute to chronic low‐grade sterile inflammation, fibroblast mechano‐sensing and responsiveness to growth factors are altered, and vascular endothelial cells progressively lose metabolic and vascular homeostatic functions (Angelini et al. 2023; Ferrucci and Fabbri 2018; Pesce et al. 2023). In humans, features of cardiovascular inflammaging are also sex‐related: men generally experience an earlier and more linear functional decline, whereas women often exhibit accelerated vascular dysfunction and fibrosis after menopause, contributing to a higher prevalence of heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (Fopiano et al. 2025).

Single‐cell and spatial transcriptomic mouse heart atlases have already documented age‐related transcriptional changes in multiple cell types (Morsy et al. 2026; Schaum et al. 2020; Tabula Muris Consortium 2020; Tabula Muris Consortium et al. 2018; Vidal et al. 2019). Large‐vessel and perivascular niches in the aging left ventricle were specifically identified as prominent sites of inflammatory, fibrotic, and senescence‐associated changes (Rodriguez Morales et al. 2025). To extend these observations, we monitored the aging response of the entire heart using bulk RNA‐seq and characterized macrophages and fibroblast‐lineage cells using single nucleus RNA‐seq and spatial transcriptomics in 6‐ and 24‐month‐old C57BL/6J male and female mouse hearts (Figure S1). Spatial transcriptomic analysis of longitudinal cardiac sections encompasses all four chambers, valves, and proximal great vessels. Our findings shift the focus from distributed sites of aging throughout the myocardium toward sites of cardiac connective tissue and large‐vessel compartments, implicating valves and aorta as niches where the strongest inflammaging‐related changes are localized. Interestingly, resulting senescence‐associated transcriptional signatures from young and aged fibroblasts partially shared features also found in the human heart.

All animal experiments were performed according to the NIH Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals and were approved by The Jackson Laboratory's Animal Care Use Committee. Inbred male and female 6‐ and 24‐month‐old C57BL/6J (n = 3 per sex and time point) were obtained from The Jackson Laboratory, maintained at a 12 h (6 AM‐6 PM) light/dark cycle with ad libitum access to water and standard chow (6% fat/kcal, 5KOG LabDiet, St. Louis, MO). Mice were sacrificed between 9 AM and 11 AM by cervical dislocation.

sections.title: RNA Extraction and Sequencing for Bulk RNA‐Seq

paragraphs.en: Hearts were placed immediately in RNAlater. Following thawing and mincing, half of the tissue was homogenized in BeadBug 6 prefilled microtubes (Sigma Millipore; two cycles of 90 s at speed 3000). RNA was isolated using RNeasy Plus Mini Kit (Qiagen) per manufacturer's protocol and quantified using Thermo Scientific NanoDrop Spectrophotometer. All samples passed quality control with a RIN value higher than 7 and a sequencing depth of 30 million reads per sample was generated. Libraries were prepared using KAPA RNA HyperPrep Kit Illumina Platforms v1.16, quantified by qPCR (KAPA Library Quantification Kit), and indexed using TruSeq DNA UD Indexes v2 (Illumina). Sequencing was on NovaSeq X Plus Kit (Illumina), a 10B Flow Cell with 8 lanes (300 cycles, 1250 M reads/lane). Full details: https://www.protocols.io/view/jax‐sen‐library‐construction‐using‐kapa‐rna‐hyperp‐kxygx7pjwl8j/v1?step=1.

sections.title: Bulk RNA‐Seq Data Processing and Analysis

paragraphs.en: Samples were processed using an internal RNA‐seq pipeline (https://github.com/TheJacksonLaboratory/cs‐nf‐pipelines/wiki/RNA‐Pipeline‐ReadMe) with default parameters. Raw reads were quality‐filtered and adapter‐trimmed using fastp (v0.23.2) and aligned to GRCm38 (Ensembl, v102) using RSEM (v1.3.1) with bowtie2 (v2.4.5). Alignment estimation of gene expression was performed using the Expectation–Maximization algorithm paired‐end read data. RSEM also generated gene‐level and isoform‐level expression estimates, producing gene counts, isoform counts, and BAM files for both genome‐aligned and isoform‐aligned reads. Post‐alignment quality control (QC) was conducted with FastQC (v0.11.9) and Picard CollectRnaSeqMetrics, and compiled using MultiQC. Normalization (trimmed Mean of M‐values) and differential expression analyses were done using the edgeR (v4.6.0), retaining genes with CPM > 1 in ≥ 2 samples and a generalized linear model (quasi‐likelihood F‐test, using sex, age, and their interaction term, FDR < 0.05) (Table S1). Sex was not a major overall driver specifically in the analysis of bulk RNA‐seqdata: 12 DEGs passed FDR < 0.05 with 7 of them on sex‐specific chromosomes (Table S2). Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were analyzed using KEGG pathway (Kanehisa et al. 2025) with clusterProfiler (v4.16.0) in R and Gene Ontology (GO) terms (Gene Ontology Consortium et al. 2023) (Table S3).

Co‐expressed network analysis used WGCNA R package (Langfelder and Horvath 2008, 2012) on normalized expression data and soft‐thresholding power approximating scale‐free topology. Gene modules were clustered by hierarchical clustering of the topological overlap matrix. Module‐trait relationships were assessed by correlating module eigengenes with age, sex, and their interaction (FDR < 0.05), followed by KEGG and GO enrichment. Out of 32 WGCNA modules tested, only one was significant for age (green module, FDR < 0.05) and none had FDR < 0.05 for sex (Tables S4 and S5).

Hearts were snap‐frozen in liquid nitrogen immediately after dissection, stored at −80°C until analysis, processed using 10× Genomics Chromium Nuclei Isolation Kits with RNase Inhibitor (PN‐1000494) following manufacturer's Protocol CG000505 Rev A. Hearts, sectioned into quarters, individually lysed using the Chromium lysis buffer, dissociated with a pestle, and subsequently pooled, mixed, and divided into four columns for further processing per manufacturer's instructions. Nuclei suspensions were combined, filtered through a 40 μm cell strainer and assessed for viability and concentration using the LUNA‐FX7 automated cell counter (Logos Biosystems). Nuclei suspensions with a concentration ranging from 8 × 103 and 2 × 105 nuclei/μL were accepted for downstream analysis.

sections.title: Single Nuclei Capture, Library Preparation, Sequencing, and Alignment

paragraphs.en: Single‐nuclei encapsulation, barcoding, and library preparation used the 10× Genomics Chromium X platform per manufacturer's protocol (CG000731_ChromiumGEM‐X_SingleCell3_ReagentKits_v4_UserGuide). cDNA and libraries' quality was assessed by Agilent TapeStation 4200 and Qubit Fluorometer (ThermoFisher) and quantified using KAPA qPCR; sequencing was done on an Illumina NovaSeq X+ 10B with a 100‐cycle flow cell (28‐10‐10‐90 asymmetric read configuration), targeting ~8000 barcoded cells/sample, with an average 50,000 reads/cell. Illumina BCL files were converted to FASTQ using ‘bcl2fastq’ v2.20.0.422, which were aligned to GRCm38 (GENCODE vM23, 10× Genomics mm10 reference 2020‐A) using the Cell Ranger ‘count’ pipeline (v8.0.0 or v9.0.1).

Nuclei were retained if they expressed > 200 genes, contained < 20% mitochondrial and < 25% ribosomal reads, and excluded if > 25,000 UMIs and expressed > 5000 genes; only genes detected in at least three nuclei were retained. Mitochondrial genes were excluded. After all QC steps, 116,002 high‐quality nuclei were retained. Further downstream analyses were conducted in the R environment using Seurat v4.0.1 (Satija et al. 2015). Doublets were removed using DoubletFinder (v2.0.3) with default parameters (McGinnis et al. 2019). Log‐transformation, normalization, dimensionality reduction via principal component analysis (PCA), and clustering were done in R (Seurat v4.0.1, resolution = 2); the first 50 principal components were used for UMAP embedding (n_neighbors and min_dist were set to default values) (Satija et al. 2015). Cell types were identified using cell‐specific marker genes (Wilcoxon rank‐sum test) as previously published; fibroblast subtypes were annotated based on three gene markers Gsn (stromal fibroblasts), Postn (specialized differentiated fibroblasts), and Dkk3 (fibroblasts characterized by a gene signature closely related to valve leaflets) (Forte et al. 2020; Jana et al. 2021). GO BP analyses were performed separately on significantly upregulated and downregulated DEGs using EnrichR (https://maayanlab.cloud/Enrichr/) for macrophages, Gsn + fibroblasts, and endothelial cells (adj. p < 0.05; |log2FC| > 0.36, Tables S6–S11). DEG analysis was done between Cdkn1a + and Cdkn1a − fibroblast‐lineage cells; young and aged samples combined, stratified by sex (n = 6 per sex; using the Wilcoxon rank‐sum test; adjusted p‐value < 0.05 and |log2FC| > 0.36). Cdkn1a + and Cdkn1a − nuclei were defined as those with non‐zero and zero normalized Cdkn1a expression, respectively. An interactive browser for the snRNA‐seq dataset is in development (https://jackson‐aging‐heart‐site.vercel.app/). It allows exploration of cell‐type‐specific gene expression and age‐associated changes across the 16 annotated cell types (116,002 nuclei from 6‐ and 24‐month‐old hearts; n = 6 per age group; sex‐balanced), along with derived cell‐level summaries including pathway and transcription factor activity, senescence scores, cell composition, and cell–cell communication. Analyses presented in the browser are exploratory and computed across nuclei; they are not part of the confirmatory analyses reported here.

Cell‐type proportions (young (p1) vs. aged (p2)) were compared using a two‐proportion Z‐test (independently for males and females) (Su 2024). Under the null hypothesis of no difference between proportions, the computed Z‐statistics follow a standard normal distribution, allowing for calculation of p‐values to assess statistical significance.

Hearts were fixed in 10% Neutral Buffered Formalin (24 h), processed overnight (Citadel 2000 Tabletop Processor), embedded in paraffin and stored wrapped in foil at 4°C for RNAse‐free sectioning for spatial transcriptomics.

FFPE cardiac sections were cut in the long‐axis (longitudinal) plane. Two to four 5 μm FFPE sections were obtained in RNAse‐free conditions. RNA was extracted using Qiagen's RNeasy Micro Kit (Cat. No./ID: 74004) and quantified using a Tapestation High Sensitivity RNA ScreenTape (Agilent). DV200 scores (% RNA sample > 200 bases in length, Agilent TapeStation Analysis software) > 50% was achieved for all sections.

sections.title: Visium Spatial Transcriptomics Library Preparation, Sequencing, Data Pre‐Processing, and Alignment

paragraphs.en: Each slide containing FFPE section (5 μm, ColorFrost Plus slides by Fisher) with the region of interest (ROI, 6.5 mm × 6.5 mm) was deparaffinized and hybridized with manufacturer‐provided mouse‐specific probe sets for mRNA labeling and transferred using the CytAssist (10× Genomics) onto a Visium CytAssist Slide; libraries were prepared per 10× Genomics Protocol CG000495, quantified using a Tapestation High Sensitivity DNA ScreenTape (Agilent) and fluorometry (Thermofisher Qubit), and verified via KAPA qPCR. The library final yield and concentrations ranges were 90–275 ng and 2.85–7.55 ng/μL, respectively. Pooled libraries were sequenced on an Illumina NovaSeq X+ 10B 100 cycle flow cell (28‐10‐10‐90 read configuration), targeting 100,000 read pairs/spot. Illumina BCL files for all libraries were converted to FASTQs (bcl2fastq v2.20.0.422, Illumina). Slides were H&E stained (The JAX Histology Core; details online https://doi.org/10.17504/protocols.io.6qpvr3653vmk/v1), scanned (40X, Nanozoomer, HT2.0, Hamamatsu), and analyzed by NDP software. For each tissue section and corresponding library, the whole slide brightfield and CytAssist images were aligned manually using the Loupe Browser (v6.4.1) via landmark registration. Each whole slide image was uploaded to a local OMERO server where a rectangular ROI containing just tissue was drawn via OMERO.web. OMETIFF images of each ROI were programmatically generated using the OMERO Python API. FASTQ files, the image registration JSON file, and associated OMETIFF corresponding to high‐resolution brightfield image were further processed, including alignment to the pre‐built mouse transcriptome reference m10‐2020‐A‐specific filtered probeset (v1.0.0) using Space Ranger count pipeline (v2.1.0). Following alignment with Space Ranger, the number of spots under tissue ranged from 2373 to 3973 across the samples. Sequencing depth yielded with a cohort‐wide average of 5452.75 ± 2157.41 median genes per spot and of 33,079.00 ± 24,316.42 median UMI counts per spot.

Data were pre‐processed using Space Ranger and analyzed in Seurat (v5.1.0) (Stuart et al. 2019). Spots were filtered using the StarDist tool (Stevens et al. 2022) by retaining only nuclei‐containing spots. Expression data were then normalized using the SCTransform workflow implemented in Seurat (Hafemeister and Satija 2019). Robust Cell Type Decomposition (RCTD, v2.2.1) (Cable et al. 2022) was applied to map cell‐type composition across all 12 Visium samples, using raw snRNA‐seq counts and corresponding cell‐type annotations as reference for the deconvolution analysis. In total, 88,704 nuclei from 19 distinct cell types were used as the reference. RCTD computes the mean gene expression profile for each annotated cell type in the reference dataset and subsequently uses these profiles to model each spatial transcriptomics spot as a mixture of cell types (without limiting their number in full doublet mode) and estimates the proportion of each cell type per spot. Significance of spatial enrichment for specific cell types or genes was assessed using permutation testing within each sample, then combined p‐values across demographic groups using Fisher's method (FDR‐corrected).

Cardiac regions (left and right ventricles, septum, atria, aorta, valves) in each heart section were manually annotated by consensus of 2 cardiovascular researchers. Published mouse heart‐specific senescence gene modules (Sanborn et al. 2025) were tested in this study in aged aortas. Expression of each gene (per sample) from the module was tested using a randomly generated null distribution, with subsequent p‐values aggregation across demographic groups (male/female, young/old; Fisher's method corrected for multiple testing), and visualization on a heatmap. DEG analysis was performed using FindMarkers in Seurat (v5.1.0), which performs a Wilcoxon Rank Sum test (min.pct = 0.1, logfc.threshold = 0, adj. p‐value < 0.05 and avglog2FC > 0) to compare macrophage‐containing spots with vs. without Ccl8, and Ccl8‐expressing macrophages vs. Ccl8‐expressing non‐macrophage cells. GO analysis was done with clusterprofiler (v4.14.6) (FDR < 0.05).

Human cardiac snRNA‐seq data was obtained from previously approved and publicly available datasets of non‐failing hearts from men and women of various ages (Bleckwehl et al. 2025). Cross‐species label transfer and CDKN1A expression analyses were performed in R (v4.4.1, Rocky Linux 8.10) using Seurat (v5.2.0), SeuratObject (v5.0.2), Symphony (v0.1.2), babelgene (v22.9), biomaRt (v2.62.1), dplyr (v1.1.4), purrr (v1.0.2), future (v1.34.0), future apply (v1.11.3), ggplot2 (v3.5.1), and pheatmap (v1.0.12). Mouse snRNA‐seq counts were converted into human gene identifier space by mapping mouse genes to their human orthologs (babelgene, only unique 1:1 orthologs). Matrices were restricted to shared genes and processed with Seurat (log‐normalization, selection of 3000 variable features, scaling, and PCA). A batch‐corrected human reference was constructed with patient identity as the integration covariate (Symphony, 3000 variable genes, 30‐dimensional latent space, UMAP for visualization). Mouse nuclei were projected into this reference and assigned human cell‐type labels (Annotation_2) via k‐nearest neighbor classification (k = 5). Concordance was quantified using confusion matrices and heatmaps, and visualized on the shared UMAP. Normalized CDKN1A expression was used to define CDKN1A‐positive cells (non‐zero expression) and calculate their proportion for each species and unified cell type (summarized in tabular form and barplots).

sections.title: Differential Gene Expression Between CDKN1A ‐Positive and Negative Fibroblast‐Lineage Cells

paragraphs.en: Mouse Gsn +, Dkk3 +, and Postn + fibroblasts (24,972 nuclei) and human fibroblast‐lineage nuclei (93,916 nuclei; all subclusters annotated as fibroblasts in the human atlas, including the two myofibroblast subclusters) were pooled per species. Nuclei with at least one Cdkn1a/CDKN1A UMI were defined as positive (mouse 2030 positive vs. 22,942 negative; human 4695 vs. 89,221). Counts were normalized to 10,000 per nucleus and log‐transformed (Seurat v5.2.0). Differential expression between CDKN1A‐positive and CDKN1A‐negative nuclei was performed with MAST (v1.32.0) via Seurat FindMarkers, including age, sex, sample (mouse) or patient cluster (human) and the cellular detection rate (scaled number of genes detected per nucleus) as covariates. Genes with Bonferroni‐adjusted p < 0.05 and |log2FC| > 0.25 were considered differentially expressed. GO BP over‐representation was computed separately for up‐ and downregulated genes with clusterProfiler (v4.14.4) against MSigDB C5 GO:BP gene sets (msigdbr v7.5.1), using all tested genes as background and Benjamini‐Hochberg correction (adjusted p < 0.05).

sections.title: Age‐Induced Cardiac Transcriptional Signatures Are Associated to Inflammaging

paragraphs.en: To obtain a comprehensive overview of cardiac age‐related changes in gene expression, we compared bulk RNA‐seq from 6‐ and 24‐month‐old C57BL/6J mouse hearts (both sexes) and identified 287 differentially expressed genes (DEGs, 183 up‐ and 104 down‐regulated) (Table S1, Figure S2). Inflammation and ECM remodeling were identified as the major signatures of aging, including changes in ECM‐receptor interaction, complement and antigen presentation (Figure 1A, Table S3). Weighted gene co‐expression network analysis (WGCNA) identified a single significant age‐associated module enriched in inflammatory and immune processes, including myeloid leukocyte activation and TNF‐associated cytokine production, together with cellular stress and ion‐regulatory responses (Figure 1B–D, Table S5).

To investigate age‐related transcriptional changes in cardiac cells specifically implicated in inflammaging, we compared snRNA‐seq profiles of cells from 6‐ versus 24‐month‐old whole hearts (Figure 1E). Cells were manually annotated using previously published markers (Figure S3). Age‐related changes in cell‐type composition were assessed by comparing nuclei proportions between aged and young hearts in males and females. Macrophages and Postn + fibroblasts increased with age, while Gsn + fibroblasts showed a modest increase in females but not in males (Figure 1F). Overall macrophage population was annotated using C1qa, encoding the A‐chain polypeptide of complement subcomponent C1q and a core biomarker to diverse populations of macrophages. Several established macrophage markers were examined in this population, and it was characterized by high expression of C1qc, Lyz2, Ctsb, Csf1r and low expression of Ccr2 (Figure S4). Gelsolin (Gsn) is a calcium‐regulated protein that binds to actin filaments. Gsn + fibroblasts were selected for further age‐associated analysis, given their established role in ECM production, marked by expression of decorin (Dcn) and collagen (Col1a1) (Forte et al. 2020). In line with this, Gsn + and Postn + fibroblasts formed a transcriptional continuum, with aging shifting cells toward the Postn + fibroblast‐associated state in both sexes, without implying a uniform or irreversible transition (Figure S5).

sections.title: Inflammaging Markers Are Localized to Valves and Aorta

paragraphs.en: To characterize the anatomical organization of cardiac cell populations specifically associated with inflammaging, we analyzed sections of 6‐ and 24‐month male and female mouse hearts encompassing all four cardiac chambers together with the valves, aortic root, and proximal great vessels. Aorta and valve areas had the highest estimated proportion of macrophages and Gsn + fibroblasts, as revealed by inferring proportional representation using deconvolution analysis that combines cell‐type signatures from snRNA‐seq data and spatial transcriptomic data (Visium, 10× Genomics) (Figure 2) (Cable et al. 2022).

Spatial analysis also enabled evaluation of gene expression and cell‐type composition across cardiac regions. Localization of general markers for macrophages in the valves and aorta of male and female hearts showed no significant changes in 24‐month old hearts (Figure 2A). Specifically, localized expression of C1qa was not significantly affected by age. However, expression of C‐C motif chemokine ligand 8 (Ccl8) became more prominent in the myocardium in both male and female hearts by 24 months (Figure 2A). Notably, Ccl8 is a key component of the senescence‐associated secretory phenotype (SASP) and robustly upregulated in senescent cells and aging tissues, driving chronic inflammation, immune cell recruitment, and tissue dysfunction (Sanborn et al. 2025).

sections.title: Aged Macrophages Acquire Stromal‐Associated and Inflammatory Transcriptional Changes

paragraphs.en: Further analysis of age‐associated changes across the macrophage compartment highlighted increased engagement of aged macrophages in stromal and vascular remodeling. In GO BP enrichment analysis of upregulated DEGs from the snRNA‐seq dataset, aged macrophages were enriched in biological processes such as growth factor and receptor signaling, including ERK1/2, PDGF‐, and VEGF‐associated signaling, concomitant with regulation of fibroblast proliferation and smooth muscle cell migration (Figure 3A). Analysis per‐sex revealed weaker enrichment of MAPK/Ras signaling and fibroblast proliferation‐related processes in males, while females were enriched for muscle‐ and cardiac morphogenesis‐associated processes (Figure 3B,C).

Ccl8 provided a link between the whole heart and spatial datasets. It was an age‐associated DEG in bulk RNA‐seq (Table S1) and belonged to the age‐related WGCNA module (Table S5). Ccl8‐expressing regions in the aorta were associated with granulocyte chemotaxis, myeloid leukocyte migration, humoral immune responses, ECM organization, cell‐substrate adhesion, wound healing, connective tissue development, and phagocytosis (Figures 4A–C, S6 and S7). These associations identify Ccl8 macrophages as an immune‐associated component of the broader whole‐heart aging response, consistent with inflammatory recruitment and local tissue remodeling.

sections.title: Aged Fibroblasts Are Associated With ECM Remodeling

paragraphs.en: Gene markers of fibroblast lineages and macrophages were expressed in same spots in valves and aorta (Figure 2). Gsn is a gene marker of fibroblast‐lineage cells co‐expressed with Cdkn1a (encoding p21, a cell cycle inhibitor associated with senescence) within the same spots in the aorta and valves, spatially locating Cdkn1a expression to fibroblast‐lineage‐enriched regions identified in deconvolution analysis (Figures 2B and 5B). Whereas Gsn expression in the valves and aorta of male and female hearts showed no significant changes in 24‐month hearts (Figure 2B), expression of Cdkn1a became more pronounced in the myocardium in both male and female hearts by 24 months (Figure 2B).

Aged Gsn + fibroblasts showed enrichment of GO BP involved in ECM and collagen organization, together with angiogenesis regulation, VEGF signaling, and endothelial cell migration (Figure 3A), consistent with increased stromal involvement in age‐associated tissue remodeling. Notably, sex‐stratified GO BP analysis demonstrated that ECM organization was prominent in aged male fibroblasts, whereas aged female fibroblasts were characterized predominantly by translation and protein biosynthetic processes (Figure 3B,C).

Consistent with Cdkn1a + spatial expression, Cdkn1a + Gsn + fibroblasts were more abundant in aged hearts (Figure 5A). Cdkn1a was also co‐expressed with Gsn (fibroblast marker) in valves and aorta (Figure 5B). Cdkn1a + Gsn + fibroblasts displayed GO enrichment of biological processes associated to growth factor‐responsive signaling, including TGF‐β‐ and PI3K‐associated processes, and regulation of miRNA metabolism and transcription (Figures 5C and S8, Table S12). These findings suggest that Cdkn1a expression is associated with altered growth factor signaling and transcriptional regulation in fibroblasts. When analyzed per sex, significant enrichment in Cdkn1a + fibroblasts was restricted to males and included miRNA regulation, growth‐factor responses, and regulation of cell migration (Figure 5D,E). No significantly enriched GO BP were identified in females due to limited overlap of upregulated DEGs with existing terms.

sections.title: Cdkn1a + Fibroblast‐Lineage Cell Programs Are Partially Conserved in Human Hearts

paragraphs.en: To assess the clinical relevance of mouse transcriptional profiles, we performed cross‐species alignment against a snRNA‐seq non‐failing human heart atlas comprising samples from various ages (Bleckwehl et al. 2025; Litvinukova et al. 2020). Transcripts in mouse cell types exhibited strong concordance with corresponding human cell populations, with 100% of mouse macrophages and 78.1% of mouse dendritic cells aligned with human myeloid populations whereas 76.2% of mouse Gsn + fibroblasts and 100% of mouse Postn + fibroblasts and 80.1% of Dkk3 + fibroblasts aligned with human fibroblast population, consisting of nine fibroblast‐lineage subclusters including myofibroblast subpopulations (Figure 6A).

GO analysis of human CDKN1A + fibroblast‐lineage populations showed upregulation of cellular stress and cell death programs, including cellular response to stress, programmed cell death, and tissue development, alongside a strongly significant cytokine response process (Figure 6B), with no biological process significantly enriched among downregulated DEGs. Conservation of upregulated GO BP between mouse and human Cdkn1a + fibroblast‐lineage populations was partial: of 381 GO BP terms enriched in mouse and 322 in human, 140 were shared (36.7% and 43.5%, respectively), led by programmed cell death, regulation of cell death, cellular response to stress and tissue development (top 12 terms displayed, Figure 6C), accompanied by upregulation of p53 target genes in both species (MDM2, ZMAT3 and EDA2R). Nonetheless, the majority of enriched processes was not shared between the two species. In summary, comparison of CDKN1A‐expressing human and mouse fibroblast‐lineage cells identified partial conservation of age‐related changes rather than a uniform cross‐species signature.

In this study, we describe spatially and cellularly resolved signatures of macrophages and fibroblasts (key immune and stromal components of cardiac inflammaging) converging on the valve/aortic root from which inflammation‐ and senescence‐associated signals extend into the myocardium with age. Bulk RNA‐seq and WGCNA established inflammation and ECM remodeling as the dominant transcriptional signatures of the aging heart. Single‐nucleus profiling further defined macrophages as an expanding population and core driver of cardiac inflammaging, with Gsn + fibroblasts appearing to represent a precursor state along a continuum toward the Postn + phenotype rather than a fixed, discrete lineage. Spatial transcriptomic analysis provided evidence supporting that cardiac inflammaging is not a diffuse, heart‐wide process but one anchored in specific anatomical niches from which it progressively encroaches on the myocardium. These observations suggest that coordinated macrophage and fibroblast responses potentially extend the concept of an immune‐fibrotic interconnected network by placing it within a defined anatomical context.

Enriched GO BP findings point toward macrophage‐fibroblast interaction and mutual activation being central to age‐related remodeling. Aged macrophages upregulated growth‐factor and stromal signaling pathways (PDGF, VEGF, ERK1/2) alongside genes promoting fibroblast proliferation, while aged fibroblasts reciprocally upregulated ECM/collagen organization and angiogenesis programs. Analysis of Cdkn1a + Gsn + fibroblasts further identified a transcriptional profile enriched for TGF‐β‐ and PI3K‐associated processes. These complementary molecular programs are consistent with the idea of a macrophage‐fibroblast communication circuit promoting stromal remodeling in the aging heart, similar to reciprocal interactions previously described during cardiac fibrosis and pathological remodeling (Guarnieri and Turley 2026; Zhang et al. 2025).

The spatial data encompassing all four chambers, valves, and proximal great vessels provide this paper's most distinctive contribution to prior aging atlases (Schaum et al. 2020; Tabula Muris Consortium 2020; Vidal et al. 2019), anchoring cell populations anatomically and revealing enrichment of macrophages and Gsn + fibroblasts in valves and the aortic root. This extends previously described vascular/perivascular aging niches (Rodriguez Morales et al. 2025) to valvular and proximal aortic regions and is consistent with these regions serving as resident niches for immune and ECM‐remodeling activity during age‐related dysfunction (Mammoto et al. 2022; Scott et al. 2021). Aging did not amplify general macrophage and fibroblast markers, with C1qa and Gsn remaining spatially constant. Instead, aging was marked by region‐specific changes including an age‐related increase in Cdkn1a + Gsn + fibroblasts and Cdkn1a expression concentrating in the valve/aorta niche. Aortic enrichment of Ccl8 added anatomical specificity to its previously reported association with profibrotic macrophage vascular niches in the aging heart of 18‐month‐old hearts, where it also drove age‐related enrichment of immune cell migration, granulocyte chemotaxis and ERK1/2 signaling consistent with our findings (Rodriguez Morales et al. 2025). Notably, both Ccl8 and Cdkn1a became more prominent in the myocardium with age. The non‐uniform, regional expression of these senescence‐associated markers (Sanborn et al. 2025; Saul et al. 2022) suggests that senescence hallmarks (Gorgoulis et al. 2019) may represent localized, spatially defined changes rather than a diffuse, whole‐organ property. This distinction may be an important refinement to the conceptualization of cardiac inflammaging. Collectively, these observations extend previous studies, positing that inflammaging originates from senescence‐associated gene expression that accumulates preferentially in specific locations. Whether this focal expression reflects a locally contained process or contributes to broader systemic effects remains an open question.

Inclusion of both sexes at 24 months, a stage underrepresented in prior transcriptomic resources (Schaum et al. 2020; Tabula Muris Consortium 2020; Vidal et al. 2019), provided insight into sex‐dependent molecular features of advanced cardiac aging. Sex‐divergent patterns of aged fibroblasts from the entire heart revealed the engagement of specific molecular programs: males showed ECM/collagen and MAPK/Ras‐dominated signatures, including a male‐restricted Cdkn1a + fibroblast enrichment, while females were characterized more by cardiac morphogenesis and protein biosynthetic/translational processes. This is consistent with clinical observations that cardiac aging in men declines earlier and more linearly while women show later, accelerated post‐menopausal decline (Calvo‐Lopez et al. 2024), suggesting that these differing clinical trajectories may map onto distinct fibroblast transcriptional programs rather than a shared profile evolving at different rates.

Cross‐species comparison provided compelling evidence of strong alignment between mouse and human myeloid and fibroblast populations. Conservation of specific upregulated biological processes in CDKN1A + fibroblast‐lineage cells (notably cellular stress‐ and cell death‐ associated programs) supported the relevance of the mouse model to human cardiac aging. However, fewer than half of the enriched processes were shared between species, indicating that senescence‐associated transcriptional programs are only partially conserved, tempering the direct translation of mechanistic findings from mouse to human.

Fibroblasts and macrophages independently emerged as cellular ‘aging hubs’ in a large‐scale human plasma proteomic study, with fibroblast aging ranking among the strongest cell‐type‐specific predictors of incident heart failure (Ding et al. 2026). These convergent human proteomic findings corroborate orthogonal support, at the protein level and in an independent species, for a role of the macrophage‐fibroblast axis in cardiac aging identified transcriptionally in our aging mouse model. While the present study is limited to transcriptomic characterization, validation of proteins of interest is an important future direction. Currently, we are developing a cardiac panel based on Cell DIVE Imaging (Gerdes et al. 2013), a multiplex platform that simultaneously detects and localizes multiple proteins within whole heart tissue sections by antibody‐based detection, to examine presence of proteins of interest, such as p21 (Figure S9).

Together, these results support a model in which cardiac aging is amplified within a valve/aortic macrophage‐fibroblast niche, with senescence‐associated molecular features, including Ccl8 and Cdkn1a, becoming progressively more prominent in the broader myocardium with age. These responses propose distinct sex‐specific molecular patterns and conservation of selected features in human tissue. The study reinforces the concept of inflammaging as a systemic, reciprocal process, refining where that process possibly initiates and how it changes anatomically, supporting a valve/aortic niche model rather than a uniform myocardial one. Moving beyond correlative evidence, determining whether this niche is a site of origin for inflammaging, rather than merely a site of detection, will require functional intervention, such as senolytic clearance of Cdkn1a + fibroblasts or blockade of Ccl8. Further studies will be needed to establish these cell types as causal drivers of age‐related cardiac dysfunction rather than markers of a broader aging process.

figures.caption: Age induces cardiac inflammation and remodeling changes and increases number of macrophages and Postn + fibroblasts. (A) Enriched KEGG pathways based on significant bulk RNA‐seq DEGs between young (6 m) and aged (24 m) mice (males and females combined; n = 3 per sex/age); FDR < 0.05; color scale (blue to red)—adjusted p value. (B) Significant age‐related module from weighted gene co‐expression network analysis (WGCNA); FDR < 0.05 (n = 3 per sex/age). (C) Expression heatmap of genes in the module from (B); color scale (green‐black‐red)—gene expression (lcpm‐log of counts per million). (D) Enriched GO BP (FDR < 0.05) based on genes in the age‐related WGCNA module. (E) Cardiac nuclei segregated according to cell types on the uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) embedding plot; combined young (6 m) and aged (24 m) males and females (n = 3 per sex/age); each point is a single nucleus, color represents cell type, Wilcoxon rank‐sum test. (F) Age‐related changes in cell composition: Nuclei count ratios (log2 ratio, aged/young) for each cell type in males and females; two‐proportion Z‐test (*p < 0.05, **p < 0.01, ***p < 0.001).

figures.caption: Aorta and valve areas had the highest estimated proportion of macrophages and Gsn + fibroblasts. figures.caption: Aging macrophages and Gsn + fibroblasts acquire stromal‐associated and ECM remodeling transcriptional changes, respectively. figures.caption: Ccl8 is significantly correlated with aged male aorta and is associated with inflammation and ECM remodeling. figures.caption: Cdkn1a+ Gsn+ fibroblast numbers increase with age and Cdkn1a+ expression is predominant in valves. figures.caption: Cross‐species integration revealed conserved biological processes between human CDKN1A + and mouse Cdkn1a + fibroblast‐lineage cells. (A) Mouse/Human alignment map of cardiac cells (quantified using confusion matrix); color scale (blue‐yellow)—aligned percentage (%); human fibroblast population consisted of nine fibroblast‐lineage and two myofibroblast subpopulations.
